newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Most Asia stocks up but Nikkei hit by BOJ comment.
newsitem.headline: Most Asia stocks up but Nikkei hit by BOJ comment.

text.p: Most Asian stock markets rallied on Wednesday in response to the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision not to raise interest rates, and some set records along the way.

Hong Kong stocks surged in early trade, with the Hang Seng Index rising more than one percent to a record 14,398.55 before surrendering gains to close marginally lower. Brokers said profit-taking emerged after the rates news was digested.
The U.S. Fed's decision added momentum to the Thai market, which surged 3.31 percent on the back of a 50 billion baht ($US1.9 billion) government support fund.
Manila's bourse finished 1.58 percent higher, and Seoul, Sydney and Taipei all recorded healthy gains.

But Tokyo stocks ignored the Fed, losing 2.41 percent after being rattled by comments by the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) deputy governor that the central bank was considering the right timing to raise the official discount rate, brokers said.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index eased 0.68 of a point to close at 14,235.52 after hitting a record high of 14,398.55.

"Stocks rose earlier on the rates news but after taking a second thought people found this has been priced in," said Franco Tong, in institutional sales at New China Hong Kong. "The market has been overbought and should come down a bit."
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average ended 490.85 points lower at 19,841.98, the lowest close since May 9 when it was 19,802.78.

A strengthening yen had prompted a sell-off in stocks of blue-chip exporters but the Nikkei's decline accelerated in late afternoon when BOJ Deputy Governor Toshihiko Fukui commented on the official discount rate, brokers said.

"The BOJ comment came at a time when the market was on edge about a rate raise, due to recent media reports that the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was in favour of a rate hike, and it startled both foreign and domestic investors into selling," said Hisao Suzuki, Yamaichi Securities deputy general manager.

The policy-setting arm of the U.S. Federal Reserve, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), on Tuesday ended weeks of debate in world financial markets with its decision to leave the key federal funds rate unchanged at 5.50 percent.
The decision brought the Dow Jones industrial average out of negative territory and enabled Wall Street to close 74.58 points, or 1.03 percent, higher at 7,303.46.
In Thailand, the government's efforts to prop up the market with a 50 billion baht support fund were beginning to revive investors' interest in the market, brokers said.
The Fed's decision also helped push stocks up 19.09 points to 596.19, they said.

"Investors are gaining more confidence in the market as they believe the support fund would help the market to a certain level. And (the Fed's) decision... was more good news," said Bunsom Kesapradist of Asia Credit.

In Manila, stocks snapped out of a four-day losing streak and rallied in light trading aided by the absence of a Fed rate hike and positive economic news. The key index ended up 39.59 points, or 1.58 percent, at 2,538.97.
"That's (interest rates) one problem out of our system. But we still have to see if we can sustain this rally," said Poch Zamora, a dealer at Peregrine Securities in the Philippines.
South Korean stocks closed at a six-month high as foreign buying in heavyweights supported the index, brokers said.
But the immediate shock from rumours of a financial crisis at the Haitai Group hurt shares in companies that have actively expanded their business in recent years, they said.
The composite index closed 3.04 points, or 0.41 percent, higher at 737.71, the highest since November 21.
Australian stocks set records in early trade but fell victim to profit-taking later in the day. The All Ordinaries Index closed 12.5 points, or 0.49 percent, higher at 2,543.2.
Taiwan shares added 26.14 points, or 0.33 percent, to end at 8,022.89.
Markets in Singapore and Malaysia were closed for a holiday.
